How the checkpoint works

The test you know.
The two parts around it.

The written test hasn't changed. This page is about the other two parts: the dictation, which happens at every checkpoint, and the speaking task, which you run when you want to hear the class speak. At the end, the two Gamefik missions open this term.

WhenHow longDoes it count?
Written test On the checkpoint day 35 to 50 minutes Yes. It is the checkpoint grade.
Dictation Always At a different time, with its own sheet About 5 minutes No. It tells you what to review in class.
Speaking Optional During the written test, one pair at a time 4 minutes per pair: 1 to read, 3 to talk In its own field, the Speaking field in the portal.
01

Dictation

Twelve items from the units in the checkpoint, heard and written down. It doesn't go into the grade. It shows you, in five minutes, which words and sentences the class still can't spell.

What's on the sheet

e.g.
One example, already written in. It has no audio: it only shows the students what to do.
1 to 9
Nine single words from the vocabulary of the units.
10 to 12
Three full sentences, using the grammar of the units.
Extra
Blank lines for words you choose. They are not on the audio: you say them yourself.

How to run it

The audio is inside the teacher's page of each checkpoint, one track per item. Play a track once, let the class write, and play it again as many times as you need.

The words themselves are not written on the teacher's page, on purpose. That page is usually on the projector, and the answers would be on the wall.

What to do with it

The teacher's page lists the mistakes that usually show up in each dictation. In Kids 4, Checkpoint 1: weigh loses the gh, pharmacy is written with an f, and stomachache comes out as two words.

If a student gets many wrong, tick the dictation block in their support plan. The plan tells them how to practice at home.

The dictation is never part of the grade.It is a diagnostic. If you use it as a test, students start guessing instead of listening.

02

Speaking

An optional task for when you want to hear the class speak. Two students, two cards, and a question neither of them can answer alone. It runs while the rest of the class does the written test, so it doesn't cost a lesson.

How the task works

Each student gets a card with two short stories. Their own story is complete: they answer from it. Their partner's story has three gaps: they fill them by asking.

At the end, the pair writes one answer together, in English. The answer needs one fact from each card, so they have to talk to get there.

The rule that makes it work: nobody shows their card. If one student reads their story out loud, the other just copies, and nobody speaks.

How the card guides them

1 · Your story
Complete. A person icon and you answer: this is where they look when their partner asks.
The clock
On story 1. One minute to read it first, in silence, before anyone asks anything.
2 · Partner's story
With gaps. A speech bubble and you ask: the answers are on the other card.

Under each title, one line in Portuguese says the same thing, for the students who need it.

Before the first speaking: a practice round

The most common problem is not the English. Students don’t understand that the two stories are different, and that their partner has the complete version of the one with gaps. So they don’t know why they should ask.

In the lesson before the first speaking, spend fifteen to twenty minutes on a practice round. It doesn’t count.

  1. Kai and Maya do the task in six panels, from the minute of silent reading to the final answer. Show it one panel at a time and ask: who has the complete story here?
  2. Show the two cards on the board. Click a gap on Kai’s card, and the answer lights up on Maya’s. That’s the idea they were missing.
  3. Model it with one student, then hand out the printed practice cards and let the pairs finish.

Kai and Maya don’t belong to any level, so the same comic works from Kids 2 to Kids 6.

On the day

  1. BeforeSet a small table in a corner, close enough to hear, far enough not to lead. Have the class grid (page 4) and a pen.
  2. CallWhile the class writes the test, call one pair. Give one card to each.Take one card each. Don't show it to your partner.
  3. 1 minEach student reads their own story in silence. The card has a clock on story 1 to remind them.Read your story in silence: one minute.
  4. GoNow they talk.Now ask. Three minutes.
  5. If stuckPoint at the first gap. Don't give them the structure.Start here. Ask your partner.
  6. If one readsStop it once. If it happens again, the pair doesn't get point 5.Only answer the question.
  7. 3 minClose the task and check what they wrote.Time. Read me the whole text, and show me your answer.

Mark while they talk, not afterwards. In forty minutes you hear twelve students without stopping the class.

The five points

  1. 1
    Asks, not only answersAsks their partner at least two questions.
  2. 2
    Uses the structure of their own storyShows up when they answer.
  3. 3
    Uses the structure of their partner's storyShows up when they ask.
  4. 4
    Fills in the gapsTwo of the three correct. Spelling doesn't count against them.
  5. 5
    Reaches the answer, in writing and in EnglishA point for the pair: both get it or neither does.

One point each. No half points. Ticked or not ticked. The student's score is the number of ticks on their line, from 0 to 5.

Points 1, 2 and 3 are for each student. You heard it, or you didn't.

Pronunciation and small grammar slips don't count against them. What counts is whether they used the structure while speaking.

Where it goes: the Speaking field in the portal, separate from the written test and the listening.

The questions to expect

The answer key on page 4 shows two questions for each gap. The first is the form the unit teaches: that one you can ask for. The second is one step further: a bonus.

1Is it because nobody eats there?or Why can’t it be the food?nobody eats there
2Did the smell start last week?or When did the smell start?last week

Any question that gets the information counts, even if it isn't on the list.

If someone asks whether this is worth the trouble

The format isn’t ours. It is two practices from the Cambridge exams, put together.

Speaking in pairs
B2 First and C1 Advanced are taken with another candidate, and Part 3 is a collaborative task between the two of them. C2 Proficiency moved to the paired format in 2002. Even A2 Key for Schools starts its second part with a card each and a conversation between candidates.
The information gap
A2 Flyers has two tasks built on exactly this: Find the Differences and Information Exchange. The definition is the one we use: the student is missing something and has to talk to get it.
Why not just a discussion
An information gap is not an opinion gap. If both students already have everything, they can agree and finish. Here the answer doesn’t exist on one card alone, so the asking isn’t optional.

What the paired format gives you

In an examiner-led interview the adult leads and the student answers. In a pair, the two speak as equals and the language is built between them — which is the thing the written test cannot show you.

The one fair objection

Research on paired tests is clear that proficiency, personality and how well the two know each other all affect an individual’s score. That is a reason to think about who you put together, not a reason to drop the task.

One difference worth naming: in Flyers the gap is between child and examiner. Ours is between two children, which is harder — and closer to what they will face at B2.

What to print

Each checkpoint is one four-page PDF. Print by page range. Every page says, at the top, how many copies you need.

PageWhat it isCopies
1Student A's cardOne per pair
2Student B's cardOne per pair
3How to run and mark itOne, for you
4Class grid and answer keyOne per class

You can type the students' names into page 4 before printing.

03

Gamefik missions

Two missions are open right now, for Kids and Teens. Students do them outside class, but they will ask you about them in class. This part tells you what each mission asks and what your role is.

EIC is a gamified school. Missions are how students earn coins outside the lesson, on top of the attitudes you launch at the end of each class. When a student asks about a mission, point them to the poster on the wall and to the Gamefik app.

Art Gallery

800 coins

Our Art Gallery has empty walls. This month's theme: a character from a book or a movie. Students draw the character and write, in English, the text that goes next to the artwork on the wall.

Two versions

Kids
Meet My Character. A drawing of the character and a short museum label for it.
Teens
Character Study. A portrait of the character and the wall text that goes beside it. The best texts make visitors stop and read.
Theme
Changes every month. The poster on the wall always shows the current one.

How you guide them

The drawing is the hook. The English is the mission. When a student shows you their work, look at the text first.

If they're stuck, help them choose the character by talking about it in English: who is it, where is it from, why this one. What they say out loud is usually the first draft of the label.

Scene Lab

1000 coins

In groups of two to four, students pick a situation from what their class is studying, write it as a real script, rehearse, and film it in one take. Deadline: Friday, 30 October.

By level

KidsTeens
Video30 to 60 seconds60 to 90 seconds
Unit expressionsAt least 3, circledAt least 5, underlined
Script in handAllowedNo paper while filming
Group2 to 4 students, one take, no cuts

Your part

  1. Send them to the front desk. That's where they pick up the script sheet. It shows how a script is written and has the lines for theirs.
  2. Read the script before they film. Correct it, hand it back, and tick Script reviewed in the teacher's check at the bottom of the sheet.
  3. They film and upload. The video and a photo of the script go to Gamefik.
  4. Close it on the sheet. Tick Filmed and sent and Mission accomplished, then sign and date. That signature is the proof for the 1000 coins.

Read the script before the camera, not after.Scripts that arrive on the last day can't be checked. If a group brings one late in October, tell them so.

04

Mural EIC

The board where we ask the front desk for things and where the front desk tells you what's happening. It replaces the WhatsApp messages that get lost: every request has a deadline, a name and a state, and nothing depends on someone remembering to scroll back.

Where it lives

Open it in the browser and pick your face. There is no password: you choose who you are, and everyone can see who asked for what.

eic-mural.web.app

Chrome and Edge offer to install it. Once installed it behaves like an app, with its own icon, and it notifies you on the computer when something of yours is ready.

Where things go

Mural The wall. Requests you send to the front desk — printing, colour copies, a room, an event — and notices the front desk sends to all of us. Choose who it's for, set a deadline, attach the file.
Balcão Printer The front desk's work queue, ordered by deadline. Your request moves through pending, doing, ready, collected. When it turns ready, it's on the counter.
Agenda One calendar for the school: checkpoints, events, room bookings and dated notices. You see every school event, and your own checkpoints. Click a day to read the details.
Links The addresses we open every day, as cards with covers: Basecamp, the checkpoints portal, forms, material. Anyone can add one.
Recados Short messages that disappear on their own after 24 hours. For running late today, not for anything that needs a deadline or an answer.
Modo TV The screen in the teachers' room. It shows what's urgent and what's ready to collect, in large type, and updates by itself.

The checkpoint, from end to end

This is the part that concerns you most. Tell us the checkpoint in the Agenda — which one, which class, which day, what time — and the whole cycle happens on the board.

  1. You schedule it. Checkpoint number, class, day and time. It appears in the calendar with your face on it.
  2. The front desk prints and hands it over. Two states, so you always know whether it's printed and whether it's waiting for you.
  3. You apply it, and mark applied on the card.
  4. You write the report in the portal, and mark report ready. That is how we know it's done: no message needed.
  5. The front desk sends it to the families. The cycle closes and the checkpoint leaves the queue.

Reports go in the usual place: eic-checkpoints.web.app. The board only records that it's ready.

You see your own checkpoints. The queue and the calendar are filtered to you, so the other classes don't get in the way. The front desk sees everything.

Every request carries a deadline and a name. That's the whole point: nobody has to ask whether it was seen.

Finished items disappear. A collected request goes after a day; a closed checkpoint moves to concluded and clears out later. The board stays short.

Attachments open inside the app, with a print button, so you don't have to download anything to check a page.

If it has a deadline, it goes on the mural.Recados are for what can be forgotten tomorrow. Everything the front desk has to do belongs on the wall, where it has a state.

In one line

Written test
Gives the grade.
Dictation
Shows what to review.
Speaking
Lets you hear what the test can't.

Questions about a specific checkpoint? The teacher's page of each one has the answer key, the audio, and the mistakes that usually show up. Anything for the front desk — printing, a room, a date — goes on the mural.
